subject: ss-hepatology
title: Hepatitis A and E: Key Concepts for NEET-PG and INI-CET

steps.tx: **Hepatitis A virus** (HAV) is a small RNA picornavirus spread by the **faecal-oral route**, often through contaminated water or food. It causes acute self-limited hepatitis and never becomes chronic. The incubation period averages about 30 days. Diagnosis rests on **IgM anti-HAV**, which appears early and marks acute infection. IgG anti-HAV appears in convalescence and gives lifelong protection.
steps.say: Hepatitis A virus is a small RNA picornavirus spread by the faecal-oral route, often through contaminated water or food. It causes acute, self-limited hepatitis and never becomes chronic. The incubation period averages about thirty days. Diagnosis rests on IgM anti-HAV, which appears early and marks acute infection. IgG anti-HAV appears in convalescence and gives lifelong protection.

steps.tx: **Relapsing hepatitis A** is a recognised variant in which jaundice and transaminases improve, then rise again within weeks to months. It is usually benign and does not progress to chronic disease. Breastfeeding is not contraindicated in mothers with hepatitis A. Standard supportive care is enough, and antivirals are not needed.

steps.tx: **Hepatitis E virus** (HEV) is a small RNA virus with four main genotypes that behave differently. Genotypes 1 and 2 infect only humans, spread by the **faecal-oral** route through contaminated drinking water, and drive outbreaks in low-resource settings. Genotypes 3 and 4 are **zoonotic**, reaching people through undercooked pork or game, and usually cause isolated cases. In **immunocompromised** patients, particularly transplant recipients, genotype 3 may persist and progress to **chronic hepatitis**.

steps.tx: **Hepatitis E in pregnancy** is especially dangerous. Case-fatality rises to about **10 to 20 percent** in the third trimester, compared with 1 to 2 percent in the general population. Vertical transmission is reported between 23.3 and 50 percent. Fulminant hepatitis is more likely in pregnant women. Management is supportive, and early specialist referral is key.
